name: Quinine skin bleaching

card.summary: Quinine appears in reports of unregulated skin-lightening products, but no research supports it as a lightening agent and its documented effects are those of an antimalarial drug.
card.note: Documented only as an ingredient reported in some illicit lightening products; quinine itself is a prescription drug with serious adverse effects.

quick.overview:
Quinine is a bitter alkaloid from cinchona bark, best known as an antimalarial drug and as a flavouring in tonic water. Wikipedia's skin-lightening article mentions that, in a 1997 Paris trafficking case, some users turned to products containing corticosteroids or quinine alongside mercury- or bleach-based preparations.

The sources reviewed contain no studies of quinine for skin lightening, and standard references on quinine do not describe a cosmetic use.
quick.mechanism: No lightening mechanism is described in the sources. Quinine's established action is against malaria parasites, where it is thought to interfere with their handling of heme.
quick.risks: Quinine at therapeutic levels can cause cinchonism (ringing in the ears, headache, nausea, vision changes) and, rarely, serious blood and heart-rhythm problems. It is prescription-only in the US, UK, Canada and Australia. Unregulated lightening products have been reported to contain other hazardous agents such as mercury and potent steroids.

lead: Quinine is a cinchona alkaloid, first isolated from cinchona bark in 1820, used to treat malaria and as a bitter flavouring in tonic water [1][2]. Its appearance-related interest comes from a passing mention in descriptions of unregulated skin-lightening products: Wikipedia reports that in a 1997 trafficking case in Paris, users of lightening products used preparations containing corticosteroids or quinine, as well as mercury- or bleach-based ones [3].

No clinical studies of quinine as a skin-lightening agent were found, and the sources reviewed do not describe a cosmetic mechanism. Clinical literature on quinine concerns malaria and related uses [1][2].
infobox: Prescription-only in US, UK, Canada, Australia
Reported in unregulated products; not studied

paras: Skin lightening is a widespread practice in parts of Africa, Asia and the Middle East, and the products used range from regulated cosmetics to unregulated preparations containing hydroquinone, corticosteroids or mercury [3]. Quinine is mentioned in this context only briefly, as one of the agents users in a 1997 Paris case were reported to use [3].
Standard descriptions of quinine do not list skin lightening among its uses [1][2].

No studies found. Published human trials of quinine concern malaria, for example comparisons of artesunate with quinine in severe malaria in African children [4], and pharmacokinetic and interaction studies in healthy volunteers.

Quinine's common adverse effects (cinchonism) include headache, sweating, nausea, ringing in the ears, hearing impairment, dizziness, blurred vision and altered colour perception; serious effects include low platelet counts, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, long QT syndrome and arrhythmias, and severe allergic skin reactions including Stevens-Johnson syndrome [2]. It also increases sunburn risk [2].

The US FDA banned over-the-counter marketing of quinine for nocturnal leg cramps in 1994 and in 2010 warned of life-threatening effects from off-label use [2]. These reports concern oral drug use, not topical cosmetic products.

Other lightening agents reported in unregulated products carry documented harms: mercury has been linked to neurological and kidney problems, and long-term hydroquinone or steroid use to skin and systemic effects [3].

timeline.event: Pelletier and Caventou isolate quinine from cinchona bark [2].
A Paris trafficking case is reported in which lightening products with corticosteroids or quinine were used [3].
